newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SOUTH AFRICA SAYS ZAIRE TALKS TO GO AHEAD.
newsitem.headline: SOUTH AFRICA SAYS ZAIRE TALKS TO GO AHEAD.

text.p: South Africa said on Saturday a delayed seaborne summit between Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila would take place later in the day.
On the battlefront, Kabila's rebels captured Mobutu's birthplace at Lisala and marched on his huge jungle palace at Gbadolite, Western security sources said.

With the rebels mustering men and materials for a final push on Zaire's capital Kinshasa, South Africa's President Nelson Mandela remained on board a converted icebreaker in Congo in the hope of bringing the two civil war rivals together.
"All the outstanding problems have been resolved," South African deputy foreign minister Aziz Pahad told reporters on the SAS Outeniqua, moored in Congo's port of Pointe Noire.

"Both parties are now satisfied that all the necessary arrangements have been made and sometime this afternoon the meeting will take place," he said. "I am glad we have overcome remaining obstacles. Things are on track."

Kabila, who failed to show for planned talks on Friday citing security concerns, left Angola's capital Luanda by plane on Saturday and a senior Western diplomat said he was apparently on his way to the summit.
"We believe Kabila has left Luanda and is on his way to meet Mobutu," the diplomat told Reuters. Officials on the ship had no update on Kabila's movements.
Mobutu, who left the ship late on Friday, spent the night at a Congolese government villa on the Pointe Noire seafront. He had yet to return to the ship on Saturday morning.

South African officials said Mandela and Mohamed Sahnoun, the U.N. and Organisation of African Unity special envoy on Zaire, held talks early on Saturday before Sahnoun left, apparently to see Mobutu.
Kabila, who remained in Angola's capital Luanda on Friday while Mandela and Mobutu sailed into international waters to meet him, criticised security and negotiating arrangements.

"If we wanted to we could win this militarily in two weeks. Suggestions that I am stalling for time are ridiculous. I am interested in finding a peaceful solution to the problem," he told a news conference in Luanda on Friday night.

South African officials said security on the Outeniqua would be tightened to meet Kabila's concerns, with particular attention to Mobutu's bodyguards and the size of delegations. "We have got sufficient security measures," Pahad said.
Mobutu boarded the Russian-built Outeniqua in Pointe Noire with great difficulty on Friday. Unable to climb 31 steep steps, he was driven on board five hours late up a make-shift ramp.
Aged 66 and suffering from prostate cancer, he is one of Africa's most enduring strongmen, backed during the Cold War by the United States as a bulwark against Soviet communism.
He has dominated Zaire since seizing power in 1965 but his illness and the whirlwind rebel offensive have weakened his grip on the former Belgian colony.
Kabila's rebels, who took up arms in October, now control around three quarters of Zaire.
Mobutu aides say talks will focus on a peaceful transition with elections open to all. They reject suggestions that the meeting is a face-saver to allow him to stand down with dignity.

Kabila, 56, says Mobutu must go and has refused to declare a truce for the talks. "There can be no ceasefire or indeed elections in this country until Mobutu and all he represents is removed and thrown away," he said this week.
The United States, France, Belgium and Britain have troops across the Zaire River in Congo's capital Brazzaville to evacuate their nationals from Kinshasa if need be.
